title: Replacement Property Identification
name: Replacement Property Identification
metaTitle: Replacement Property Identification in Denver, CO
metaDescription: Building a working replacement property list across metro Denver so your 45-day identification window closes with real, vetted options, not guesses.

sections.html: The 45-day identification window doesn't care whether an investor has found a property yet. It starts the day the relinquished property closes and runs regardless. Our job is to have a real, checked list ready before that clock starts, built from actual Denver-area inventory rather than a broker's wish list assembled after the fact.

sections.heading: How we build the list
sections.html: We start pulling candidates as soon as an investor tells us a sale is likely, not once it's under contract. That gives us weeks, sometimes months, of lead time to track pricing, tenant quality, and seller motivation across whatever asset classes fit the investor's goals, whether that's multifamily in Aurora, net lease pads along I-25, or industrial space in the I-70 corridor. By the time closing happens, the list already reflects current market conditions instead of stale data.

sections.heading: Balancing asset classes on one list
sections.html: Colorado's Front Range in-migration keeps money moving between Denver metro and mountain resort capital in both directions, and that flow affects pricing across several asset classes at once, from DTC office to suburban retail. We rarely put all our eggs in one property type. A typical identification list mixes something with strong current cash flow, something with upside if a lender's terms come in better than expected, and a genuine backup in case the first choice falls out of contract.

sections.heading: Timing the list to the market
sections.html: Denver's fastest-moving submarkets, RiNo and LoDo multifamily especially, can put a property under contract within days. Slower-moving submarkets in the southern and western suburbs give more room to negotiate and more time to run numbers. We weight the identification list toward whichever pace matches how much runway the investor actually has left in their 45 days, since a property that needs two weeks of lender review doesn't belong on a list with only ten days left on the clock.

sections.heading: What the identification rules require in practice
sections.html:
Investors generally identify up to three properties regardless of value, or more than three if the combined value stays under 200 percent of the relinquished property's sale price, or, less commonly, enough properties to cover 95 percent of what's ultimately purchased. We keep the list structured against whichever rule the investor's advisor confirms applies, and a list usually includes a mix such as:

  • One primary candidate with strong current income and clean title
  • One backup candidate in a different submarket in case the primary falls through
  • One stretch candidate with more upside but a longer diligence timeline

sections.heading: When the list needs a real backup
sections.html: Denver's competitive submarkets mean a top candidate can go under contract to another buyer before an investor is ready to move. We treat every identification list as needing at least one genuine backup property, fully vetted and ready to step in, not a placeholder added just to fill space on the notice. That backup has closed more than one exchange when a first-choice deal fell apart late.

sections.heading: Keeping the list current through closing
sections.html:
An identification list isn't a one-time document we hand over and forget. We keep checking each candidate's status through the full 180-day period, since a property can go under contract to someone else, a lender's terms can shift, or a seller's asking price can move after the notice is submitted. Investors get an updated read on where each candidate stands rather than finding out at day one-seventy that a top pick is no longer available.

When a candidate does fall out, we go back to the original sourcing pool rather than starting from scratch, since the earlier research on comparable properties in that submarket is usually still current enough to move quickly on a replacement candidate.

We treat that fallback pool as part of the value of starting the search early. A list built weeks before closing already has runner-up candidates identified, so swapping one property for another doesn't mean starting the research from zero with only days left on the clock.

faqs.q: When does the 45-day identification window actually start?
faqs.a: It starts on the closing date of your relinquished property, not when you first start looking for a replacement. That's why we begin building a candidate list well before the sale closes whenever possible.

faqs.q: How many properties can I put on my identification list?
faqs.a: Up to three regardless of value, or more than three if their combined value stays under 200 percent of what you sold, or a smaller set covering 95 percent of what you end up buying. Your qualified intermediary and tax advisor confirm which rule fits your situation.

faqs.q: Why would I identify a backup property I don't intend to buy?
faqs.a: Denver's faster-moving submarkets can put a primary candidate under contract to someone else before you're ready to close. A vetted backup keeps the exchange alive instead of forcing a rushed decision on a weaker property.

faqs.q: Do you only source one type of property, like multifamily or office?
faqs.a: No, we typically mix asset classes on a single list depending on the investor's goals, since balancing current income against upside potential usually works better than concentrating in one property type alone.

faqs.q: What happens if none of my identified properties work out?
faqs.a: If every identified property falls through before the 180-day exchange period ends, the exchange generally fails and the sale proceeds become taxable. That's exactly why we build backup options into every list from the start.
